idiom_name: keyed handler table + lookup/invoke dispatcher (+ optional registrar)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare a table that binds keys to handlers (map for sparse, string or otherwise heterogeneous keys; array when the key space is a small dense integer range) and fill it at one place - static initialisation, module init or explicit registration - so that the table, not a branch, is the definition of the supported operations. Dispatch is then: validate the key, look it up, apply the miss policy and invoke the handler with the same arguments every time. Keep the handler contract uniform (pass a context/request object rather than varying arguments), keep the table as small in lifetime as the registry allows (module-private, frozen after startup), and decide explicitly whether unknown keys raise, fall back or are logged. The classic structure is still justified over exhaustive pattern matching when the key space is open. Test on the table, not only on the handlers - the tables that matter are the ones that can silently be incomplete.
code_sketch:
table = build_table()                # key -> handler, filled once at startup
handler = table.get(key)             # validated lookup
if handler is None:
    raise UnknownKey(key)            # one explicit miss policy
return handler(request)              # one uniform call, no branching
pitfalls: Skipping the miss policy: a silent default handler turns a typo into behaviour that 'works' but does nothing.
Registering from several places without a defined order: the table then depends on initialisation order rather than on intent.
Widening the handler signature until every entry receives an untyped bag of arguments, discarding the type safety of a switch arm.
Letting the table grow into a general service locator that resolves unrelated dependencies by string key.
Out-of-range indices with computed goto: an unchecked index can jump to an arbitrary code address, making external input an attack vector.
Unverifiable exhaustiveness: the table silently accepts a missing entry where a switch would warn at compile time.
Mutable global state: concurrent registration leads to data races; tests leak registrations into each other.

Wrong move: dispatching straight from user input through reflection (Perl can(), Python getattr) into any matching subroutine -> attackers reach unintended callables -> instead consult only an explicit allowlist table that exposes nothing beyond its registered entries.

Wrong move: hand-writing lambda bodies in the table that duplicate what named handlers should own -> table and functions drift apart and the duplication hides -> instead bind entries to named top-level functions and, where a naming convention determines the key, generate the table from the convention.

Wrong move: declaring per-handler policy (auth, arity, setup requirements) in scattered decorators or in-handler checks -> coverage cannot be audited at the dispatch site and a forgotten annotation ships an unprotected route -> instead make policy a field of the table entry and enforce it uniformly at dispatch time (git's RUN_SETUP/NEED_WORK_TREE flags; a ROUTES table pairing handlers with auth levels).
